episode_title: #16 Why 85% of AI Projects Fail - And Why Most Teams Are Still Getting AI Wrong | Greg Nudelman

real_qa.q: Why does Gartner report that 85% of AI projects fail?
real_qa.r: According to Gartner, 85% of AI projects fail not for technology reasons, but for reasons of technology alignment to customer needs and business needs. Greg Nudelman identifies this as a failure of UX practices, stating that AI projects fail because of lack of good UX practices and that the 85% failure rate is fundamentally a UX failure, not a technology failure.
real_qa.requete: why 85 percent AI projects fail Gartner

real_qa.q: What is the Snowball Sprint methodology for building AI products?
real_qa.r: Snowball Sprint is an extension of the old design sprint concept that starts with framing the problem before writing any code, using use case, data, and value exercises. The process includes quick RAG file design on paper, vibe coding a solution, then rapid iterative testing with actual AI prototypes in front of customers. It takes about a week or two to complete, producing a customer-validated prototype that becomes the shipped product without requiring a complete recode, eliminating handoffs and accelerating development.
real_qa.requete: Snowball Sprint AI product development methodology

real_qa.q: What does the value matrix exercise measure in AI projects?
real_qa.r: The value matrix, authored by Orjansson Gupta who created Salesforce Einstein, assigns cost or benefit to each outcome (true positive, false positive, true negative, false negative) and multiplies that by how often the outcome actually occurs. This helps determine the real-world impact of AI decisions—a very accurate AI can be completely useless if it leaves money on the table, such as a 99.99999% accurate TSA screening model that always returns false and misses actual threats.
real_qa.requete: value matrix AI outcomes cost benefit Salesforce Einstein

real_qa.q: Why do companies fail when adopting AI without proper use case definition?
real_qa.r: The wrong use case is the primary reason that torpedoes the majority of AI projects. Teams must understand what problem they are solving, what the job to be done is, what pain they are addressing, how it is currently being done, and what AI will bring that is not being done today. This should be done collaboratively as a storyboard exercise taking 15-20 minutes with the team, identifying where the AI interaction happens, what the interaction is between AI and customer, and what the outcome should be.
real_qa.requete: AI project failure wrong use case definition

real_qa.q: What training is Greg Nudelman providing for designers and product managers in AI?
real_qa.r: Greg has created the UX4AI Professional Certification program based on his book UX4AI, which teaches designers and product managers how to apply fundamental UX skills to AI projects. The program is available at UX4AI.com and the first cohort completely sold out at South by Southwest. He emphasizes that designers need to take a program that will teach confidence and ability to refocus existing skills in customer satisfaction and jobs to be done onto AI projects.

real_qa.q: Why is the Hadoop comparison relevant to current AI adoption in enterprises?
real_qa.r: Greg compares current AI adoption to the Hadoop syndrome, where boards demanded AI without understanding what to use it for, just like they demanded Hadoop when it first came out without knowing its purpose. The key difference is that with AI, the technology is genuinely transformative and real, unlike Hadoop which was often a branding exercise. However, boards are pushing AI adoption without allocating sufficient training budgets for internal teams to understand and properly implement these technologies.
real_qa.requete: Hadoop syndrome AI adoption enterprise boards
